headline: Astronauts make fastest American trip to space station

sources.title: Historic SpaceX Crew-13 Launches to Space Station from Florida (AP, via WDTV)
SpaceX's Crew-13 reaches space station in record-fast trip as mission begins (FOX 35 Orlando)
SpaceX smashes US record as astronauts reach ISS in just 7 hours and 55 minutes (Interesting Engineering)
SpaceX Crew-13 docks with International Space Station after record-fast flight (video, WKMG News 6)

chunks.text: Four astronauts {{blasted off}} from Florida on Thursday morning, October 1, 2026. Their SpaceX capsule {{closed in on}} the International Space Station that evening. It {{linked up with}} the station 7 hours and 55 minutes after launch, a new US record. The launch had been {{pushed back}} three weeks to repair a [[leaking]] [[fuel system]]. There were [[thick clouds]] that morning, but the weather {{cleared up}} in time.

verbs.correct: To start a flight to space
verbs.why: Most rockets blast off from Florida or California. A space shuttle blasts off with a loud roar. Four astronauts blasted off from Florida on Thursday morning.

verbs.correct: To get closer and closer to something
verbs.wrong: To send radio messages to someone
verbs.why: As our plane closes in on the airport, we see the city lights. Fishing boats close in on the harbor just before dark. Their SpaceX capsule closed in on the International Space Station that evening.

verbs.correct: To join together with another spacecraft
verbs.wrong: To fly in a circle around a planet
verbs.why: A supply ship links up with the station every few months. A small boat links up with the big ship far from shore. The capsule linked up with the station 7 hours and 55 minutes after launch.

verbs.correct: To move an event to a later date
verbs.why: Airlines often push back flights in bad weather. Our team pushes back the meeting to Friday when the boss is away. The launch was pushed back three weeks to repair a leaking fuel system.
It often rains in the morning and clears up after lunch. The sky usually clears up before sunset. There were thick clouds that morning, but the weather cleared up in time for the launch.

chunks.text: The old US record was 12 hours and 33 minutes, set by a Dragon [[cargo]] capsule in November 2024. The best time for a US crew was 14 hours and 43 minutes. The station was in a good position at launch. The capsule started to {{catch up with}} it almost right away. A SpaceX official said the team got lucky and the timing {{worked out}}. A Russian crew still holds the [[overall record]], at just over three hours.

verbs.correct: To reach a moving thing from behind
verbs.wrong: To turn slowly in a circle
verbs.why: I walk ahead, and my friend catches up with me at the park. A fast runner catches up with the leader on the last lap. The station was in a good position, so the capsule started to catch up with it almost right away.

verbs.wrong: To stay the same for years
verbs.why: Most moves are stressful, but they usually work out. Things often work out well for hard workers. A SpaceX official said the team got lucky and the timing worked out.

chunks.text: The crew's [[commander]] is a NASA [[geologist]] who once worked on a [[Mars rover]]. She is the first Black woman to command a crew in [[orbit]]. The other three are new to space. They are a NASA pilot who is a retired Marine, a Canadian [[air force colonel]] and a Russian former [[submarine officer]]. They will {{take over from}} four astronauts who arrived in February. For six months, they will do research and {{look after}} the station.

verbs.correct: To replace someone at a job
verbs.wrong: To visit someone for a day
verbs.why: A daughter often takes over from her father at the family store. The night nurse takes over from the day nurse at seven. The new crew will take over from four astronauts who arrived in February.
My neighbor looks after my plants while I'm away. My sister looks after our grandmother on the weekend. For six months, the new crew will do research and look after the station.

chunks.text: The crew {{played up}} the number 13. Their [[mission patch]] [[honors]] Apollo 13, the 1970 [[Moon mission]] that ended safely. They {{headed out}} to the [[launch pad]] in black cars with "Lucky 13" [[license plates]]. The Canadian astronaut's wife is due to have their third child in late November. NASA says it will help him {{keep up with}} family events. Hours after the launch, SpaceX {{sent up}} over 100 small satellites from California.

verbs.correct: To give extra attention to something
verbs.wrong: To give a new name to something
verbs.why: The ad plays up the car's low price. Coaches play up their team's strong defense. The crew played up the number 13, with a patch that honors Apollo 13.

verbs.wrong: To guard a place at night
verbs.why: We head out to the beach early on Saturdays. Most workers head out at five. The crew headed out to the launch pad in black cars with "Lucky 13" license plates.
She reads the news every day and keeps up with world events. Busy parents rarely keep up with their old friends. NASA says it will help the Canadian astronaut keep up with family events.

verbs.correct: To launch a rocket or satellite
verbs.wrong: To build something in a factory
verbs.why: The country sends up a new weather satellite every few years. Space agencies send up telescopes to study distant stars. Hours after the crew launched, SpaceX sent up over 100 small satellites from California.

mainIdea.s: A SpaceX capsule took four astronauts from Florida to the space station in under eight hours. Due to the station's good position, it was the fastest trip ever by an American spacecraft.
mainIdea.why: The crew arrived 7 hours and 55 minutes after launch. The station was in a good spot, so the capsule could catch up with it right away.

mainIdea.s: Four astronauts reached the orbiting lab less than eight hours after launch, a new US record. SpaceX says a new and more powerful rocket engine made the short trip possible this time.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the trip was fast because the station was in a good position at launch. A SpaceX official said the timing worked out.

mainIdea.s: A NASA crew has come home to Earth after six months on the space station. Their capsule landed safely in the ocean, and doctors are now checking how the long stay affected them.
mainIdea.why: This story is about a crew that has just arrived at the station. They blasted off on October 1 and set a new US speed record.

tf.s: The crew's capsule linked up with the station in record US time.
tf.why: It linked up with the station less than eight hours after launch, a new US record.

tf.s: The launch went ahead on its first planned date, with no delays.
tf.why: The launch had been pushed back three weeks to repair a leaking fuel system.

tf.s: The capsule started to catch up with the station almost right away.
tf.why: The station was in a good position at launch, so the timing worked out.

tf.s: The crew now holds the overall record for the fastest trip to the station.
tf.why: The crew linked up faster than any US crew, but a Russian crew still holds the overall record.

tf.s: The new crew will take over from astronauts who arrived in May.
tf.why: The four astronauts they will take over from arrived on the station in February.

tf.s: The new crew will do research and look after the station.
tf.why: For six months, the four astronauts will live on the station and do research there.

lines.text: Did you hear about the astronauts who {{blasted off}} from Florida on Thursday?
I saw the launch. Did they reach the space station yet?
Yes, the same evening. They made the trip [[in record time]], just under eight hours.
Eight hours? That's about as long as my workday. How did they do it?
[[The stars aligned]]. The station was in a good spot at launch, so the capsule could {{catch up with}} it almost right away.
That's what a SpaceX official said. Their capsule {{closed in on}} the station that evening and arrived a little after seven.
Yeah, they {{pushed it back}} three weeks to fix a fuel leak.
And the crew really {{played up}} the number 13. They even had "Lucky 13" license plates.
Apollo 13 made it home safely, so maybe 13 is a lucky number. [[Knock on wood]].
There's a sweet detail, too. The Canadian astronaut's wife is having a baby in late November.
While he's in orbit? So he won't be there for [[the big day]]?
Not in person. But NASA says it will help him {{keep up with}} family events.
What will the crew do on the station for six months?
They'll {{take over from}} four astronauts who got there in February. They'll do research and {{look after}} the station.
Sounds like a busy six months.

expressions.def: Used to say something was done faster than ever before
ex: She finished the puzzle in record time.
The team built the bridge in record time.

expressions.def: Used to say that everything happened at the right time, as if by luck
ex: We found a house and a job in the same month. The stars aligned.
The weather was perfect and the band was great. The stars aligned that night.

expressions.def: Used to say it is good that something happened, even if it was late
ex: He finally called me back. Better late than never.

expressions.def: Said after you talk about your good luck, to hope that the luck will continue
ex: I haven't been sick all year, knock on wood.
Our old car still runs well. Knock on wood.

expressions.def: A very important day, like a wedding or the day a baby is born
ex: They have been practicing for months, and the big day is Saturday.
On the big day, the whole family went to the hospital.
